clue.text: South America imports tea, for example

indicators.note: to import is to bring in, so the tea goes inside the other letters

parts.note: US, the United States, stands for America
cha is an informal British word for tea

explanation.surface: A continent bringing in shipments of tea, offered as an example of trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South America' looks like one place, but 'America' gives the abbreviation for the United States; 'imports' signals the container. CHA is British slang for tea.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase introduces an instance, exactly as 'for example' does: 'fruits such as apples'.

clue.text: Doctor Who's day to have confrontation

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with or alter, so the letters of the word are rearranged

parts.note: to own something is to have it

explanation.surface: Doctor Who, the time-travelling TV hero, gets a day to face down an enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor Who' is the BBC science-fiction series, but here 'Doctor' is the anagram signal rearranging WHO'S into SHOW.
explanation.definitionFit: A decisive face-off between two rivals is a synonym for a confrontation.

clue.text: Character essential to Archimedes?

indicators.note: what is essential to something sits at its core, so the letters lie inside the name

explanation.surface: Asks which quality was central to the great Greek mathematician's personality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests personality, but it means a letter; the question mark nods to Archimedes being Greek, fitting a Greek letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A character is a letter of an alphabet; this one is the twenty-second letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Maybe bitter old lady providing fish

parts.note: bitter is a kind of beer, an example of ale, hence 'maybe'
'the old lady' is slang for one's wife

explanation.surface: A pub scene: a drink of bitter, perhaps, for the old woman, who supplies a fish supper.
explanation.walkthrough: BITTER is British draught beer, a type of ale; 'old lady' is British slang for a wife.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a North American herring-like species that runs upriver to spawn.

clue.text: Sweep outside a B&B, using mop?

indicators.note: the swinging word is placed outside, around the other letters

parts.note: a sweeping movement of the arm or bat is a swing
bed and breakfast, written as two Bs

explanation.surface: Someone cleaning the pavement in front of a guesthouse, wondering if a mop is the tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweep' looks like part of the cleaning picture, but means a swinging stroke; 'outside' makes it the container. B&B is a British bed-and-breakfast guesthouse.
explanation.definitionFit: To swab a floor or deck is to clean it with a mop, so the verb form means cleaning with one.

clue.text: Cheeky lad beat a paparazzo?

parts.note: to beat with a lash is to whip
per means 'a', as in 'ten pounds per hour'
a press photographer, informally a snapper

explanation.surface: An impudent boy thrashes a celebrity photographer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' reads like the article but gives PER, as in 'so much a day'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names an impudent, presumptuous young person, often a boy.

clue.text: Promise to marry little woman, admitting corruption

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the decay goes inside the name

parts.note: Beth March is one of the sisters in Louisa May Alcott's novel Little Women
rot is decay or moral corruption

explanation.surface: A man pledges to wed his wife, though the arrangement lets some corruption in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little woman' sounds like a patronising term for a wife, but points to Beth from Little Women.
explanation.definitionFit: To pledge someone in marriage, or to engage oneself to wed, is the meaning of this verb.

clue.text: Lack of consistency in crying out for reform

indicators.note: to reform is to reshape, so these letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Accuses campaigners of being inconsistent when they shout out demands for reform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' looks like it could be the anagram signal, but it is part of the fodder; 'for reform' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Being out of keeping or not fitting together is lacking consistency or harmony.

clue.text: Festival axes many stars

parts.note: a gala is a festive occasion
the x and y axes of a graph

explanation.surface: An event cancels its big-name celebrity line-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'axes' looks like a verb, cancels, but stands for the X and Y axes of a graph.
explanation.definitionFit: A huge system of stars bound together, such as the Milky Way, is this astronomical body.

clue.text: Playing mostly forte, take sonata very fast

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters being performed in a new order
mostly means all but the last letter is kept

explanation.surface: A musician tackles a sonata at loud volume and at a brisk tempo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims FORTE to FORT; 'Playing' then rearranges FORT, TAKE and SONATA together.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom from the speed of ships, measured in knots, meaning briskly or rapidly.

clue.text: Novel having unexpected outcome, by Hardy?

parts.note: Oliver Hardy, of the comedy duo Laurel and Hardy
a twist is a surprising turn in a story

explanation.surface: Describes a book with a surprise ending, written by Thomas Hardy perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' suggests the novelist Thomas Hardy, but it is the comedian Oliver Hardy; the book is by Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of Charles Dickens's second novel, about a workhouse orphan.

clue.text: Officer briefly gets depression

definitions.meaning: the short form of the rank colonel
a dip between two mountain peaks, used as a pass

explanation.surface: An army officer, curtly described, is feeling low.
explanation.definitionFit: It abbreviates a military rank and also names a low saddle in a ridge between summits.

clue.text: Swim by breakwater? That's relatively crazy

parts.note: a dip is a quick swim
a pier can serve as a breakwater against waves

explanation.surface: Someone thinks taking a swim beside the harbour wall is rather mad.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of 'dippy', silly or daft, so it means more crazy than another.

clue.text: Execution by necessity involves attendant

indicators.note: to involve is to include, so the attendant goes inside

parts.note: perforce is an old word meaning of necessity
a manservant or attendant is a man

explanation.surface: Sounds like a grim note that an execution must, by law, include an attendant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Execution' suggests a hanging, but means the carrying out of a task.
explanation.definitionFit: Execution can mean the carrying out or rendering of a task or piece, which is a synonym.

clue.text: What arises from the Ashes? Renewed hope, having heard scores

indicators.note: made new again, so the letters are refashioned in a new order
heard signals that the word is spoken, giving a sound-alike spelling

parts.note: to score a surface is to nick it

explanation.surface: Cricket talk: after the Ashes series, revived hope as the crowd hears the scores.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ashes is the England–Australia cricket series; the capital A hides the mythical bird reborn from its own ashes.
explanation.definitionFit: In myth this bird burns itself and is reborn from the ashes of its own pyre.

clue.text: It's where Elgar, at the end, worked with score

definitions.text: It's where Elgar, at the end, worked with score

indicators.note: worked as in kneaded or manipulated, so the letters are reshaped
the final letter of the composer's name is taken

explanation.surface: Points to the place where the composer Elgar spent his later years writing music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worked' rearranges IT'S WHERE, R (Elgar's last letter) and SCORE. Elgar was born near Worcester and much of his work was written there.
explanation.definitionFit: This English county in the West Midlands was Edward Elgar's home and inspiration.

clue.text: Spurs having nightmare? It's a delicate case

parts.note: to egg someone on is to spur them, so 'spurs' is 'eggs'
a nightmarish experience is hell

explanation.surface: Tottenham Hotspur, known as Spurs, endure a dreadful match, a sensitive matter.
explanation.walkthrough: Spurs is the nickname of Tottenham Hotspur football club, but here it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The thin brittle shell around an egg is a fragile container, hence a delicate case.

clue.text: What's needed to make orange grange useless?

parts.words: What's needed to make orange grange
parts.note: putting G in place of O changes one word into the other; G is good and O is nothing (zero), so G for O

explanation.surface: A riddle about the change that turns a fruit into a farmhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: G stands for good and O for nothing (zero), so swapping O for G reads 'good for nothing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Describes a worthless idler, someone of no use at all.

clue.text: Old copper spilt petrol, a tiny bit of it?

definitions.text: Old copper spilt petrol, a tiny bit of it?

parts.note: d was the symbol for the old British penny, a copper coin

indicators.note: spilt suggests the letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A retired policeman has spilt petrol, perhaps just a drop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old copper' suggests a retired policeman, but means the pre-decimal British penny, written d.
explanation.definitionFit: A single small drop of a liquid is a tiny amount of spilt petrol.

clue.text: One who tries hugging quiet bar employee

indicators.note: hugging means holding inside, so the quiet letter is enclosed

parts.note: one who tries food or drink is a taster
p, piano, is the musical mark for quiet

explanation.surface: A wine taster cuddles a silent barman.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who draws beer from the taps in a pub serves at the bar.

clue.text: Disagreement after detailed article portrays economy

indicators.note: after means the quarrel comes behind the shortened word
de-tailed, with its tail or last letter cut off

parts.note: the definite article
a rift is a split or quarrel

explanation.surface: A detailed newspaper article about a falling-out describes the economy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' reads as 'thorough', but splits as de-tailed, removing the last letter of THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Careful management of money and resources is frugality, which is what economy means.

clue.text: Where you may find kipper and meat to scoff

parts.note: ham is cured pork, a meat
to scoff at is to mock

explanation.surface: A breakfast table where smoked fish and meat are wolfed down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kipper' suggests the smoked herring, but means a sleeper (kip is British slang for sleep); 'scoff' suggests eating, but means mock.
explanation.definitionFit: A swinging bed of net or canvas is where someone having a kip may lie.

clue.text: Fruit juice about to net a profit

indicators.note: to net is to catch, so the reversed word encloses the rest
about suggests turning round, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: sap is the juice of a plant
to pay is to be profitable, so profit as a verb

explanation.surface: A juice-maker hoping to turn a profit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reverses the juice to give PAS; 'to net' (catch) makes that the container, and 'profit' works as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: These are tropical melon-like fruits with orange flesh, also called pawpaws.

clue.text: Local independent news

parts.note: read as 'new' twice, N plus N, since N abbreviates new

explanation.surface: Neighbourhood stories in an independent newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' is British slang for one's nearby pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A neighbourhood pub, or 'local', is a hostelry, and so is a tavern of this kind.

clue.text: Plant abundant on bogs is from France

indicators.note: on means the abundant word is placed after the others

parts.note: bog and loo are both British slang for toilet
est is French for 'is'
rife means widespread or abundant

explanation.surface: A plant grows abundantly on French marshland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bogs' suggests marshes, but means toilets in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a flowering plant, the purple or yellow kind often found by water.

clue.text: Head off burning rage

indicators.note: removing the head means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: burning as a noun, a blaze

explanation.surface: A furious person storms off in a burning temper.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words name intense anger or wrath.

clue.text: Essay returning model aircraft, originally in box?

indicators.note: in means the reversed letters go inside

parts.note: box is a type of evergreen tree

indicators.note: returning means coming back, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: to model for an artist is to sit

indicators.note: originally means only the first letter is used

explanation.surface: A paper about a model aeroplane flown back in its box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' reverses the model plus the aircraft's first letter, giving ATIS; 'in' places it inside a box, which is a kind of evergreen.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal written discourse on a subject is a lengthy essay.

clue.text: Ring true about daughter's nasty experience

parts.note: O looks like a ring

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the true word goes around

parts.note: real means genuine or true
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A telephone call confirming a daughter's painful trial.
explanation.definitionFit: A painful or trying experience is a trial or tribulation.
